scene.testo: Step outside the station and the temperature drops to minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit. Step into the sunlight and it jumps to plus 250. Same astronaut, same suit, a few seconds apart. So how do astronauts survive without a single heater?

Imagine you are floating inside the International Space Station at 6 AM. The alarm chimes. The air feels comfortable, around 72 degrees Fahrenheit. Yet just inches beyond the wall, the vacuum of space is waiting to freeze you solid.

You unzip your sleeping bag, which is clipped to the wall. You drift toward the galley. Outside the window, Earth rolls by at 17,500 miles per hour. You will circle the planet about 16 times before the day ends.

The station orbits roughly 250 miles above Earth. That is about the distance from New York City to Washington, D.C., but straight up. At that height there is almost no air, so almost nothing carries heat away from you.
Here is the first surprise. Space itself is not really cold in the way you imagine. Cold needs something to touch you and steal your warmth. In a vacuum, there is almost nothing to do the stealing.
Think of a thermos bottle. A vacuum between two walls keeps your coffee hot for hours. Space works the same way. A warm object in a vacuum cannot lose heat by touching air, because there is no air.

On Earth, heat escapes three ways. Conduction, through touch. Convection, through moving air. And radiation, through invisible infrared light. In orbit, the first two nearly vanish. Only radiation is left, and that changes everything.
So the real danger on the station is not freezing. It is the opposite. Every person aboard gives off roughly 100 watts of heat. Add computers, lights, and pumps, and the station wants to cook itself.

That is why the International Space Station does not mainly need heaters. It needs a giant cooling system. Pumps push liquid ammonia through loops outside the station, carrying heat away from the crew modules.

Those radiators are the big flat panels you can see on the truss. They dump waste heat into space as infrared light. Your body heat, your laptop heat, your dinner heat, all of it leaves the station as glowing infrared.

Now imagine the sun. Every 90 minutes the station completes one lap around Earth. Roughly every 45 minutes, it swings from blazing daylight into total darkness. Sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets, every single day.
In direct sunlight, the outside of the station can climb past 250 degrees Fahrenheit. In Earth's shadow, it can plunge toward minus 250. That swing is a brutal test for metal, wires, and seals.
To survive it, the station wears a coat. Layers of thin, shiny insulation wrap its modules. It looks like crumpled gold foil. You have seen the same material in a marathon runner's emergency blanket.

These blankets are called multi-layer insulation. Many thin films are stacked with gaps between them. Each layer reflects heat back where it came from. In a vacuum, that simple trick works astonishingly well.
Now put yourself on a spacewalk. You are sealed in a suit that weighs about 300 pounds on the ground, heavier than a grand piano keyboard cabinet. In orbit, it weighs nothing, but it still has mass.
The suit is not a heater. It is a tiny spaceship shaped like a person. It holds oxygen, removes carbon dioxide, and keeps pressure around your body. And, above all, it controls your temperature.

Under the hard outer shell, you wear a garment laced with thin plastic tubes. Cool water flows through them. It is called a liquid cooling and ventilation garment, and it looks like long underwear covered in spaghetti.

Why cooling, not heating? Because working hard in a sealed suit makes you hot. A spacewalk can last more than six hours. Your muscles generate heat, and without sweat evaporating freely, that heat has nowhere to go.

The water carries your heat to a backpack unit. There, a device called a sublimator lets ice turn straight into vapor in the vacuum. That process pulls heat away, and your suit gets cooled by space itself.
Still, some parts of you do get cold. Your fingers and toes are the weak spot. Astronauts have described cold hands during spacewalks, especially when gripping a cold handrail in the shade.

The gloves have small heaters built into the fingertips. Yes, heaters. So the title has a catch. Spacewalkers do use a little electrical warmth on their hands. But the main battle is controlling heat, not making it.

Outside the suit, the rules get strange. Touch a metal tool sitting in sunlight and it can be hot enough to damage a glove. Touch the same tool in shadow and it can be dangerously cold. Context is everything.

So the suit is built in many layers. Inside, a comfortable liner. Then the cooling garment. Then a pressure bladder. Then restraint fabric. Then insulation. Then a tough outer layer. It is like a very advanced winter coat.

The outer layer is white for a reason. White reflects sunlight. A dark suit would absorb heat and cook its owner. That is why you rarely see a dark spacesuit outside a spacecraft. White is nature's sunscreen.

Back inside the station, life is far more relaxed. Crews wear shorts and T-shirts most days. Imagine eating breakfast in a T-shirt while orbiting 250 miles above the planet. Not what most people picture.

Breakfast might be rehydrated scrambled eggs and a tortilla. You squeeze hot water into a pouch. You wait a few minutes. Then you eat with a spoon, carefully, because a floating blob of egg is a real hazard.
Your own body is a heater. A person at rest gives off about 100 watts. That is the same as an old incandescent light bulb. Seven crew members make about 700 watts, enough to keep a small room warm.

On Earth, warm air rises. On the station, it does not. With no gravity, the air around you stays put. Your own warm breath can wrap around your face like a bubble. Fans must keep air moving constantly.

Without fans, a crew member sleeping in a quiet corner could breathe in her own carbon dioxide and wake up with a headache. So fans run all day and all night. That steady hum is the sound of the station.
Now think of sleep. You slide into a bag tied to the wall. No pillow, no mattress, because there is no down to press against. You zip up, and the fabric keeps you from drifting into a vent or a wall.

The cabin stays near room temperature. Crews can adjust it a bit, and different modules run slightly different. Astronauts have said the Russian side can feel a little different from the American side. Small details, but real ones.

Compare that to a camping trip on Earth. At 20 degrees Fahrenheit, you pile on a down jacket, wool socks, and a heavy sleeping bag. Meanwhile, the station crew sleeps comfortably in shorts, just a thin bag away from a vacuum.

Now go back to the Apollo era. Spacecraft heading to the Moon turned slowly, like a chicken on a rotisserie. NASA called it passive thermal control. The slow roll spread the sun's heat evenly across the whole ship.
Without that slow spin, one side would bake while the other froze. Engineers did not invent a miracle machine. They used a slow, steady roll, about one turn every hour, to share the sunshine fairly.

On the lunar surface, the numbers get more extreme. In daylight, the Moon's surface can reach about 250 degrees Fahrenheit. At night, it falls to roughly minus 280. Apollo astronauts walked only in the lunar day.

Apollo moonwalkers wore suits with cooling garments too. Water flowed through tubes against their skin. After hours of work in lunar dust and sunlight, the cooling water was the only thing keeping them comfortable.

And then came Apollo 13. On April 13, 1970, an oxygen tank failed. The crew moved into the lunar module, a lifeboat built for two people, and shut down nearly everything to save power. The ship got cold.

Crew accounts say the temperature dropped to near freezing, around 38 degrees Fahrenheit in places. Water condensed on the walls. They wore whatever they had and tried to sleep. That is what a spacecraft does when the heat is gone.

They had shut off power on purpose. Every watt mattered, and electronics make heat. With almost everything off, the cabin simply cooled down. It was a rare case where the crew truly needed a warmer room.

So what about spacecraft that do need warmth? Satellites and rovers carry small electric heaters, plus insulation. Some deep space probes use a tiny amount of radioactive material that gives off steady warmth for years.

On the station, thermal engineers work around the clock. Mission control in Houston watches temperature sensors across the whole station. If a pump slows or a loop leaks, they know within seconds, and the crew can respond.

One real emergency shows how fragile it is. On July 31, 2013, an astronaut's helmet filled with water during a spacewalk, in part because of a cooling system problem. The walk ended early, and everyone made it back inside.

That day proved that cooling is life support. The suit's water loop is not a luxury. When something in that loop goes wrong, a six hour job can become an emergency, with the crew racing back to the airlock.
Compare it to your home. Your furnace burns fuel to add heat. The station does the reverse. It spends its whole life getting rid of heat. Your house fights the cold. The station fights the warmth.

So how do astronauts survive the cold of space without heaters? Mostly, they do not fight cold at all. They fight heat. Insulation, white coatings, water loops, and giant radiators keep everything balanced.

And here is the most surprising part. The warmest object in that frozen darkness is you. Your body, glowing in infrared at about 100 watts, is the heater. The whole station is just carefully managing your warmth.

descrizione:
How do astronauts survive the freezing cold of space without heaters? The answer surprises almost everyone. In this Orbital Days documentary, we float inside the International Space Station and step outside on a spacewalk to explore temperatures swinging from -250°F to +250°F.

You will learn why space is not cold in the way you think, how the station sheds heat with ammonia loops and giant radiators, how spacesuits use cooling water instead of heaters, and how Apollo crews handled the extremes, including the cold cabin of Apollo 13.

All facts come from NASA and astronaut accounts. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more questions about daily life in orbit.
